claim: Virulent T. gondii strains secrete kinases and pseudokinases that inactivate the immunity-related GTPases (IRG proteins) responsible for mouse resistance to avirulent strains.
source: Virulent T. gondii strains secrete kinases and pseudokinases that inactivate the immunity-related GTPases (IRG proteins) responsible for mouse resistance to avirulent strains.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and is consistent with established knowledge in the field.

claim: The mouse IRG system shows extraordinary polymorphic complexity in the wild.
source: We report that the mouse IRG system shows extraordinary polymorphic complexity in the wild.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequencing data and phylogenetic analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: An IRG haplotype from a wild-derived mouse strain confers resistance against virulent parasites by interference with the virulent kinase complex.
source: We describe an IRG haplotype from a wild-derived mouse strain that confers resistance against virulent parasites by interference with the virulent kinase complex.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing resistance in CIM mice and mechanistic studies.

claim: In resistant hosts, virulent strains can encyst.
source: In such hosts virulent strains can encyst, hinting at an explanation for the evolution of virulence polymorphism in T. gondii.
evidence: This claim is supported by cyst counts in CIM mice infected with virulent strains.

claim: The sexual process of T. gondii occurs in true cats (Felidae).
source: The sexual process occurs in true cats (Felidae) and intermediate hosts become infected by ingesting oocysts spread in cat faeces.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dubey, 1998 and represents established knowledge about T. gondii life cycle.

claim: Intermediate hosts become infected by ingesting oocysts spread in cat faeces.
source: The sexual process occurs in true cats (Felidae) and intermediate hosts become infected by ingesting oocysts spread in cat faeces.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dubey, 1998 and represents established knowledge.

claim: A phase of fast intracellular replication and spread (tachyzoite phase) stimulates immunity in the intermediate host.
source: A phase of fast intracellular replication and spread (tachyzoite phase) stimulates immunity in the intermediate host, and this in turn induces parasite encystment in brain and muscle cells and lifelong persistence.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about T. gondii infection dynamics.

claim: Immunity in the intermediate host induces parasite encystment in brain and muscle cells and lifelong persistence.
source: A phase of fast intracellular replication and spread (tachyzoite phase) stimulates immunity in the intermediate host, and this in turn induces parasite encystment in brain and muscle cells and lifelong persistence.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about T. gondii infection.

claim: If immunity fails, tachyzoite replication continues uninterrupted, killing the infected host within a few days.
source: If immunity fails, tachyzoite replication continues uninterrupted, killing the infected host within a few days (Deckert-Schlüter et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Deckert-Schlüter et al., 1996.

claim: The probability that T. gondii completes its life cycle depends on early immune control.
source: Thus the probability that T. gondii completes its life cycle, which is roughly linear with duration of infection of the intermediate host, depends on early immune control.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between infection duration and transmission probability.

claim: Mus musculus is probably the evolutionarily most important intermediate host for T. gondii.
source: Mus musculus is probably the evolutionarily most important intermediate host for T. gondii, because it is very abundant worldwide and sympatric with a uniquely abundant felid, the domestic cat.
evidence: This is an inference based on ecological considerations.

claim: Early immune control of T. gondii in mice depends on a family of IFNγ-inducible cytoplasmic effector proteins, the 47 kDa immunity-related GTPases (IRG proteins).
source: Early immune control of T. gondii in mice depends on a family of IFNγ-inducible cytoplasmic effector proteins, the 47 kDa immunity-related GTPases (IRG proteins; for nomenclature of IRG genes and proteins see Bekpen et al. (2005); Martens and Howard (2006) and 'Materials and methods') (Taylor et al., 2000; Collazo et al., 2001; Liesenfeld et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: IRG proteins assemble on the cytosolic face of the parasitophorous vacuole membrane (PVM), causing its rupture and killing the included parasite.
source: These assemble on the cytosolic face of the parasitophorous vacuole membrane (PVM), causing its rupture and killing the included parasite (Martens et al., 2005; Zhao et al., 2009b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Martens et al., 2005 and Zhao et al., 2009b.

claim: In the C57BL/6 (BL/6) laboratory mouse strain about 20 IRG genes occur in two adjacent clusters on chromosome 11 and one cluster on chromosome 18.
source: In the C57BL/6 (BL/6) laboratory mouse strain about 20 IRG genes occur in two adjacent clusters on chromosome 11 and one cluster on chromosome 18 (Bekpen et al., 2005) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bekpen et al., 2005 and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The whole 47 kDa sequences of IRG proteins are typically translated from a single exon.
source: The whole 47 kDa sequences of IRG proteins are typically translated from a single exon.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about IRG gene structure.

claim: Certain 'tandem' IRGB proteins have a molecular weight of about 94 kDa.
source: Exceptional are certain 'tandem' IRGB proteins with a molecular weight of about 94 kDa.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bekpen et al., 2005.

claim: Tandem IRG genes are transcribed across two chromosomally adjacent IRG coding units and the intergenic spacer is spliced out as an intron resulting in a single open reading frame.
source: These genes are transcribed across two chromosomally adjacent IRG coding units and the intergenic spacer is spliced out as an intron resulting in a single open reading frame (Bekpen et al., 2005. See also 'Materials and methods' for a note on nomenclature of the tandem genes and proteins).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bekpen et al., 2005.

claim: IRG proteins fall into two major functional and sequence sub-families: the GKS group (IRGA, IRGB and IRGD proteins) that are effector proteins at the PVM, and the GMS group (Irgm1, Irgm2 and Irgm3) that are negative regulators of the GKS proteins.
source: IRG proteins fall into two major functional and sequence sub-families, the GKS group (IRGA, IRGB and IRGD proteins) that are effector proteins at the PVM, and the GMS group (Irgm1, Irgm2 and Irgm3) that are negative regulators of the GKS proteins (Hunn et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hunn et al., 2008.

claim: Many strains of T. gondii (e.g., the abundant Eurasian strains designated types II and III) are well controlled by the IRG system in laboratory mice, encyst, and are considered avirulent.
source: Many strains of T. gondii (e.g., the abundant Eurasian strains designated types II and III) are well controlled by the IRG system in laboratory mice, encyst, and are considered avirulent.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about T. gondii strain virulence.

claim: Type I T. gondii strains are highly virulent, killing the mouse host during the tachyzoite phase of infection.
source: But others (e.g., type I) are highly virulent (Sibley and Boothroyd, 1992), killing the mouse host during the tachyzoite phase of infection.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sibley and Boothroyd, 1992.

claim: Virulence differences between T. gondii strains are largely due to polymorphic variation in ROP18 and ROP5.
source: It has very recently been shown that virulence differences between T. gondii strains are largely due to polymorphic variation in ROP18 and ROP5 (Saeij et al., 2006; Taylor et al., 2006; Khan et al., 2009; Behnke et al., 2011), members of a family of kinases and pseudokinases (El Hajj et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to recent work.

claim: ROP18 and ROP5 are members of a family of kinases and pseudokinases.
source: It has very recently been shown that virulence differences between T. gondii strains are largely due to polymorphic variation in ROP18 and ROP5 (Saeij et al., 2006; Taylor et al., 2006; Khan et al., 2009; Behnke et al., 2011), members of a family of kinases and pseudokinases (El Hajj et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to El Hajj et al., 2006.

claim: ROP proteins are secreted during parasite entry and accumulate on the cytosolic face of the PVM.
source: These proteins are secreted during parasite entry and accumulate on the cytosolic face of the PVM (Boothroyd and Dubremetz, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Boothroyd and Dubremetz, 2008.

claim: Virulent ROP allotypes inactivate IRG effector proteins by phosphorylating essential threonines in the nucleotide-binding domain.
source: Virulent ROP allotypes inactivate IRG effector proteins by phosphorylating essential threonines in the nucleotide-binding domain (Fentress et al., 2010; Steinfeldt et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fentress et al., 2010 and Steinfeldt et al., 2010.

claim: Within laboratory strains there is relatively little IRG protein polymorphism on Chr 11.
source: Within laboratory strains we found relatively little IRG protein polymorphism on Chr 11.
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: Wild-derived strains showed variation in IRG gene number and remarkable protein polymorphism.
source: In contrast, the wild-derived strains showed variation in IRG gene number and remarkable protein polymorphism.
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: Irgb6 in the CAST/EiJ strain has an allele with 47 amino acid substitutions relative to BL/6.
source: For example Irgb6, a protein of 406 residues, had an allele in the CAST/EiJ strain with 47 amino acid substitutions relative to BL/6.
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data.

claim: On Chr 18, IRG protein sequence variation between laboratory strains was more apparent than on Chr 11.
source: On Chr 18, IRG protein sequence variation between laboratory strains was more apparent, and again, wild-derived strains showed extensive sequence polymorphism and copy number variation.
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: The IRG proteins of M. spretus showed considerable protein divergence from M. musculus sequences.
source: The IRG proteins of the outgroup, M. spretus, showed considerable protein divergence from M. musculus sequences.
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: Pseudogenes occurred in every IRG haplotype.
source: Pseudogenes occurred in every haplotype and some (e.g. Irga5 and Irgb7) were preserved between M. musculus and M. spretus.
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: Some IRG pseudogenes (e.g. Irga5 and Irgb7) were preserved between M. musculus and M. spretus.
source: Pseudogenes occurred in every haplotype and some (e.g. Irga5 and Irgb7) were preserved between M. musculus and M. spretus.
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data.

claim: Within a limited group of strains, eleven distinct IRG gene haplotypes on Chr 11 and thirteen on Chr 18 can be distinguished.
source: Even within this limited group of strains we can distinguish eleven distinct IRG gene haplotypes on Chr 11 and thirteen on Chr 18, already yielding a theoretical population diversity of several hundred IRG genotypes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the sequencing data presented.

claim: The nearest-neighbour phylograms of Irgm1, Irgb10 and Irga6 are shallow and the M. spretus sequences fall into outgroups.
source: The nearest-neighbour phylograms of Irgm1, Irgb10 and Irga6 are shallow and the M. spretus sequences fall into outgroups.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Most of the sparse polymorphic variation in Irgm1, Irgb10 and Irga6 has been acquired since the divergence of M. musculus from M. spretus.
source: Thus most of the sparse polymorphic variation in these sequences has been acquired since the divergence of M. musculus from M. spretus.
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The phylograms for Irgb2 and Irgb6 have a depth similar to the mouse-rat divergence (about 20 million years).
source: In contrast, the phylograms for Irgb2 and Irgb6 have a depth similar to the mouse-rat divergence (about 20 million years) (Gibbs et al., 2004), the M. spretus sequences are embedded in the M. musculus trees, and any tendency to correlation with subspecies is seen only in the outermost branches.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis and citation to Gibbs et al., 2004.

claim: The polymorphism in Irgb2 and Irgb6 is ancient and has persisted through a number of speciation events.
source: Thus the polymorphism in these two genes is ancient and has persisted through a number of speciation events.
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The scale of polymorphism in the IRG system estimated by Tajima's π from 7 mouse strains resembles that of classical MHC genes.
source: The scale of polymorphism in the IRG system estimated by Tajima's π from 7 mouse strains resembles that of classical MHC genes (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by diversity analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: There is considerable local polymorphism within geographic ranges at IRG loci.
source: That there is also considerable local polymorphism within geographic ranges was confirmed by the identification of numerous heterozygotes at all loci examined by PCR among the wild mouse captures.
evidence: This is supported by PCR data from wild mouse samples.

claim: The wild-derived Indian strain CIM is remarkably resistant to the type I virulent T. gondii strain, GT-1.
source: The wild-derived Indian strain CIM, which has a number of divergent IRG alleles (Figure 2B), proved to be remarkably resistant to the type I virulent T. gondii strain, GT-1 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: All CIM mice survived intraperitoneal infection with GT-1 tachyzoites while all laboratory mice (NMRI strain) died within 15 days.
source: All CIM mice survived intraperitoneal infection with GT-1 tachyzoites while all laboratory mice (NMRI strain) died within 15 days.
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: IFNγ-induced CIM diaphragm-derived cells (DDC) inhibited proliferation of type I virulent RH-YFP strain tachyzoites as efficiently as they inhibited the proliferation of avirulent strains.
source: By this assay, IFNγ-induced CIM diaphragm-derived cells (DDC see 'Materials and methods') inhibited proliferation of type I virulent RH-YFP strain tachyzoites as efficiently as they inhibited the proliferation of avirulent strains, while BL/6 DDC inhibited only the avirulent strains (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by 3H-uracil incorporation assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: BL/6 DDC inhibited only avirulent T. gondii strains.
source: By this assay, IFNγ-induced CIM diaphragm-derived cells (DDC see 'Materials and methods') inhibited proliferation of type I virulent RH-YFP strain tachyzoites as efficiently as they inhibited the proliferation of avirulent strains, while BL/6 DDC inhibited only the avirulent strains (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by 3H-uracil incorporation assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: IFNγ-induced CIM cells died by reactive cell death after infection with both virulent RH-YFP and avirulent ME49.
source: Additionally, IFNγ-induced CIM cells died by reactive cell death after infection with both virulent RH-YFP and avirulent ME49, while BL/6 cells died only after infection with avirulent strains (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: BL/6 cells died by reactive cell death only after infection with avirulent T. gondii strains.
source: Additionally, IFNγ-induced CIM cells died by reactive cell death after infection with both virulent RH-YFP and avirulent ME49, while BL/6 cells died only after infection with avirulent strains (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Reactive death of T. gondii-infected mouse cells after induction with IFNγ is associated with IRG protein-mediated host resistance.
source: Reactive death of T. gondii-infected mouse cells after induction with IFNγ is associated with IRG protein-mediated host resistance, as previously reported (Zhao et al., 2009b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhao et al., 2009b.

claim: Resistance of CIM mice to the type I virulent RH-YFP strain in vivo was tightly linked to the IRGCIM gene cluster on Chr 11 (p<<10−6).
source: In five independent experiments involving a total of 65 typed animals (Figure 5A), resistance by this assay was almost completely dominant and was tightly linked to the IRGCIM gene cluster on Chr 11 (p<<10−6).
evidence: This is supported by genetic linkage analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: There was no detectable association of virulence with the IRGCIM cluster on Chr 18.
source: There was no detectable association of virulence with the IRGCIM cluster on Chr 18.
evidence: This is supported by genetic linkage analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Mice homozygous for IRGCIM at the Chr 11 gene cluster were as resistant as wild-type CIM mice.
source: In a similar analysis of 53 F2 progeny, mice typed as homozygous IRGCIM at the Chr 11 gene cluster were as resistant as wild-type CIM mice.
evidence: This is supported by genetic analysis of F2 progeny.

claim: The Chr 11 IRGCIM homozygotes showed complete resistance to RH-YFP infection.
source: Assayed directly by survival, 51 backcross and F2 mice infected with RH-YFP followed the same pattern as in the peritoneal cell assay (Figure 5B), with the Chr 11 IRGCIM homozygotes (cc in Figure 5B) showing complete resistance, the heterozygotes (bc) substantial but incomplete resistance and the IRGBL/6 homozygotes (bb) complete and acute susceptibility.
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The Chr 11 IRGCIM heterozygotes showed substantial but incomplete resistance to RH-YFP infection.
source: Assayed directly by survival, 51 backcross and F2 mice infected with RH-YFP followed the same pattern as in the peritoneal cell assay (Figure 5B), with the Chr 11 IRGCIM homozygotes (cc in Figure 5B) showing complete resistance, the heterozygotes (bc) substantial but incomplete resistance and the IRGBL/6 homozygotes (bb) complete and acute susceptibility.
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The IRGBL/6 homozygotes showed complete and acute susceptibility to RH-YFP infection.
source: Assayed directly by survival, 51 backcross and F2 mice infected with RH-YFP followed the same pattern as in the peritoneal cell assay (Figure 5B), with the Chr 11 IRGCIM homozygotes (cc in Figure 5B) showing complete resistance, the heterozygotes (bc) substantial but incomplete resistance and the IRGBL/6 homozygotes (bb) complete and acute susceptibility.
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: There was 17% recombination between Irgb6 and Nlrp1.
source: We obtained 17% recombinants between Irgb6 and Nlrp1.
evidence: This is supported by genetic typing data.

claim: There was no correlation between Nlrp1 genotype and the ability to clear virulent T. gondii.
source: There was no correlation between Nlrp1 genotype and the ability to clear virulent T. gondii (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by genetic analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Nlrp1 is not detectably expressed in the IFNγ-induced DDC transcriptomes.
source: It is anyway unlikely that Nlrp1 plays a role in the resistance polymorphism we describe since it is not detectably expressed in the IFNγ-induced DDC transcriptomes (data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by transcriptome data.

claim: Two type I virulent strains, GT-1 and BK, formed cysts in CIM mice.
source: Two type I virulent strains, GT-1 and BK, formed cysts in CIM mice (Figure 5C, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by cyst counts shown in Figure 5C and Table 1.

claim: The avirulent type III strain, NED, encysted in the laboratory mice >20× more efficiently than in CIM mice.
source: The avirulent type III strain, NED, encysted in the laboratory mice >20× more efficiently than in CIM mice (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by cyst counts shown in Table 1.

claim: In BL/6 cells Irgb6BL/6 loaded onto only about 8% of RH-YFP vacuoles.
source: In BL/6 cells Irgb6BL/6 loaded onto only about 8% of vacuoles, while in CIM cells the highly divergent Irgb6CIM protein loaded onto more than 50% of vacuoles (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence quantitation shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In CIM cells the highly divergent Irgb6CIM protein loaded onto more than 50% of RH-YFP vacuoles.
source: In BL/6 cells Irgb6BL/6 loaded onto only about 8% of vacuoles, while in CIM cells the highly divergent Irgb6CIM protein loaded onto more than 50% of vacuoles (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence quantitation shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The tandem protein, Irgb2-b1BL/6, is poorly expressed in BL/6 cells.
source: Even more extreme, the tandem protein, Irgb2-b1BL/6, which is poorly expressed in BL/6 cells (Figure 6B), was not detectable on the RH-YFP PVM, while the highly divergent Irgb2-b1CIM was well-expressed in CIM cells and loaded onto over 95% of vacuoles (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Irgb2-b1BL/6 was not detectable on the RH-YFP PVM.
source: Even more extreme, the tandem protein, Irgb2-b1BL/6, which is poorly expressed in BL/6 cells (Figure 6B), was not detectable on the RH-YFP PVM, while the highly divergent Irgb2-b1CIM was well-expressed in CIM cells and loaded onto over 95% of vacuoles (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The highly divergent Irgb2-b1CIM was well-expressed in CIM cells and loaded onto over 95% of RH-YFP vacuoles.
source: Even more extreme, the tandem protein, Irgb2-b1BL/6, which is poorly expressed in BL/6 cells (Figure 6B), was not detectable on the RH-YFP PVM, while the highly divergent Irgb2-b1CIM was well-expressed in CIM cells and loaded onto over 95% of vacuoles (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and western blot data shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: In CIM cells infected with RH-YFP, phosphorylated Irga6CIM was barely detectable with an antiserum specific for Irga6BL/6 phosphorylated at T108.
source: Remarkably, in CIM cells infected with RH-YFP, phosphorylated Irga6CIM was barely detectable with an antiserum specific for Irga6BL/6 phosphorylated at T108 (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Irga6CIM differs from Irga6BL/6 at only two residues, both distant from the phosphorylation sites.
source: Irga6CIM differs from Irga6BL/6 at only two residues, both distant from the phosphorylation sites and was phosphorylated normally when transfected into IFNγ-induced L929 cells infected with virulent RH-YFP (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by sequence comparison and western blot data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Irga6CIM was phosphorylated normally when transfected into IFNγ-induced L929 cells infected with virulent RH-YFP.
source: Irga6CIM differs from Irga6BL/6 at only two residues, both distant from the phosphorylation sites and was phosphorylated normally when transfected into IFNγ-induced L929 cells infected with virulent RH-YFP (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The amount of phosphorylated Irga6 was strikingly reduced on vacuoles loaded with Irgb2-b1CIM.
source: Figure 6E,F show that the amount of phosphorylated Irga6 was strikingly reduced on vacuoles loaded with Irgb2-b1CIM while the amount of total Irga6 loaded onto Irgb2-b1CIM positive vacuoles was increased (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence quantitation shown in Figure 6E and 6F.

claim: The amount of total Irga6 loaded onto Irgb2-b1CIM positive vacuoles was increased.
source: Figure 6E,F show that the amount of phosphorylated Irga6 was strikingly reduced on vacuoles loaded with Irgb2-b1CIM while the amount of total Irga6 loaded onto Irgb2-b1CIM positive vacuoles was increased (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence quantitation shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The decreased signal of phosphorylated Irga6 on the PVM was not caused by competition for loading between Irga6 and Irgb2-b1, but rather by inhibition of phosphorylation.
source: Thus the decreased signal of phosphorylated Irga6 on the PVM was not caused by competition for loading between Irga6 and Irgb2-b1, but rather by inhibition of phosphorylation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that total Irga6 loading increased while phosphorylated Irga6 decreased.

claim: Transfected Irgb2-b1CIM stimulated the loading of endogenous Irgb6BL/6 onto RH-YFP vacuoles.
source: Transfected Irgb2-b1CIM also stimulated the loading of endogenous Irgb6BL/6 onto RH-YFP vacuoles (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence quantitation shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Transfected Irgb2-b1BL/6 had little or no effect on the loading of Irgb6BL/6.
source: Transfected Irgb2-b1BL/6, which is well expressed unlike the endogenous protein, had little or no effect on the loading of Irgb6BL/6 (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence quantitation shown in Figure 6H.

claim: The essential difference between Irgb2-b1BL/6 and Irgb2-b1CIM in determining resistance lies in the amino acid sequence polymorphism rather than in the protein expression level.
source: Thus the essential difference between Irgb2-b1BL/6 and Irgb2-b1CIM in determining resistance lies in the amino acid sequence polymorphism rather than in the protein expression level.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that transfected Irgb2-b1BL/6, which is well expressed, had little effect compared to Irgb2-b1CIM.

claim: Loading of Irgb2-b1CIM onto the PVM of ROP5-deficient RH strain parasites in CIM cells was greatly reduced.
source: Thus loading of Irgb2-b1CIM onto the PVM of ROP5-deficient RH strain parasites in CIM cells was greatly reduced, and consistently, the amount of loading on to different RH-related strains correlated with strain-specific variation in the amount of ROP5 (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The amount of Irgb2-b1CIM loading on to different RH-related strains correlated with strain-specific variation in the amount of ROP5.
source: Thus loading of Irgb2-b1CIM onto the PVM of ROP5-deficient RH strain parasites in CIM cells was greatly reduced, and consistently, the amount of loading on to different RH-related strains correlated with strain-specific variation in the amount of ROP5 (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and western blot data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Irgb2-b1CIM becomes phosphorylated during infection with virulent T. gondii.
source: Irgb2-b1CIM itself becomes phosphorylated during infection with virulent T. gondii (Figure 7B), thus is also a target for the active ROP5-ROP18 kinase complex, suggesting that Irgb2-b1CIM may block phosphorylation of Irga6 by binding ROP5 pseudokinase at the vacuole, thereby distracting rather than inhibiting ROP18 kinase.
evidence: This is supported by autoradiogram data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: ROP5 binds to Irga6 via helix 4 (H4) of the Irga6 nucleotide binding domain.
source: ROP5 binds to Irga6 via helix 4 (H4) of the Irga6 nucleotide binding domain (Fleckenstein et al., 2012), so a homologous structure on Irgb2-b1 may be involved in ROP5 interaction.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fleckenstein et al., 2012.

claim: The putative H4 and αD structural domains of the Irgb2 subunit are highly polymorphic and show recent divergent selection.
source: Indeed the putative H4 and αD structural domains of the Irgb2 subunit are highly polymorphic and show recent divergent selection (Figure 7C), indicating possible co-evolution with ROP kinases and pseudokinases.
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The IRG protein system essential for resistance against T. gondii infection in the mouse has a complex polymorphism on the scale of the MHC.
source: We have shown that the IRG protein system essential for resistance against T. gondii infection in the mouse has a complex polymorphism on the scale of the MHC, and that at least one IRG haplotype, found in the wild-derived CIM strain mouse, is strikingly resistant to T. gondii strains that are highly virulent for laboratory mice.
evidence: This is supported by the diversity analysis and phylogenetic data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Resistance of the CIM mouse against type I virulent T. gondii strains is determined by the presence of the polymorphic tandem IRG protein, Irgb2-b1CIM encoded on Chr 11.
source: We also provide a mechanistic explanation for the resistance of the CIM mouse against type I virulent T. gondii strains. Resistance is determined by the presence of the polymorphic tandem IRG protein, Irgb2-b1CIM encoded on Chr 11, which blocks the ROP5/ROP18 kinase complex of the virulent parasite, preventing phosphorylation and consequent inactivation of IRG effector proteins.
evidence: This is supported by genetic linkage analysis and functional studies.

claim: Irgb2-b1CIM blocks the ROP5/ROP18 kinase complex of the virulent parasite, preventing phosphorylation and consequent inactivation of IRG effector proteins.
source: We also provide a mechanistic explanation for the resistance of the CIM mouse against type I virulent T. gondii strains. Resistance is determined by the presence of the polymorphic tandem IRG protein, Irgb2-b1CIM encoded on Chr 11, which blocks the ROP5/ROP18 kinase complex of the virulent parasite, preventing phosphorylation and consequent inactivation of IRG effector proteins.
evidence: This is supported by phosphorylation studies and transfection experiments.

claim: Loss of the entire IRG system in several vertebrate groups, for example higher primates and birds, suggests that possession of the IRG system may be costly.
source: Loss of the entire IRG system in several vertebrate groups, for example higher primates and birds (Bekpen et al., 2005), suggests that possession of the IRG system may be costly.
evidence: This is an inference based on evolutionary patterns and citation to Bekpen et al., 2005.

claim: The close association of cat and mouse with humans has led to large-scale transformations in the ecology of T. gondii over the last 10,000 years.
source: The close association of cat and mouse with humans has led to large-scale transformations in the ecology of the parasite over the last 10,000 years.
evidence: This is speculation based on ecological and historical considerations.

claim: The patterns of genetic resistance against T. gondii in its most important intermediate hosts will determine the relative abundance of strains contaminating the environment, and thereby the strains available for human infection.
source: The patterns of genetic resistance against T. gondii in its most important intermediate hosts will determine the relative abundance of strains contaminating the environment, and thereby the strains available for human infection.
evidence: This is speculation about the implications of the findings.
